title: What not to put on the site for a developer-tool company
metaTitle: What to leave off a developer-tool site
excerpt: Cut the slogan about empowering developers. Keep a real screen of the tool and a way to try it. A shorter, truer site beats a long performance of taste.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky. The article is about refusing a grand facade when the tool itself should be the view.
caption: Height is not the same thing as a working tool. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first line to remove?
faqs.answer: Remove a slogan such as empowering developers, delightful developer experience, or built for builders. Replace it with the mechanism: what the tool reads, what it writes, and what it refuses. If the line could sit on any tool company, it is not doing work on yours.

faqs.question: What should remain after the cut?
faqs.answer: Keep a real screen or transcript and one stable way to try the product. Keep the limits, the docs, and the changelog in words engineers already use. A short site still needs those separate jobs. It does not need them restated as a manifesto.

faqs.question: How do you know a block should go?
faqs.answer: Finish the sentence, this helps an engineer, and see whether the ending is a mechanism or a mood. Mood can leave. Check the first screen on a phone after the cut. If the tool and the try path are still obvious, stop adding.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Most developer-tool company website mistakes are things you should remove. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing does not want a louder homepage. They want a real screen of the tool and a clear way to try the product. A slogan about empowering developers reassures the team and tells the reader nothing they can run. Cut it. A shorter site that shows the mechanism will beat a long site that performs taste.

Taste can stay in the type, the spacing, and the accuracy of a transcript. It does not need a manifesto, a meetup photo, or a second headline that restates the first in softer words. If a block does not help this reader understand the tool or try it, take it off the page.

## Cut the slogan first

"Empowering developers" can decorate any company in the category. So can "delightful developer experience," "built for the way you build," and "the platform for modern teams." These lines survive internal review because nobody can disagree with them. They fail the only review that matters. An engineer cannot test them.

Replace the line with the mechanism. What the tool reads, what it writes, and what it refuses. "Fails the build when a migration locks a table, and names the statement" is a line they can falsify by trying the product. Put that in the first screen. Delete the banner. You will feel the page get plainer. Plain is the correction.

Do the same to slogans that have been split into a grid. Six tiles of speed, safety, and joy are one empty sentence with icons. Keep a capability only when it sits on a real screen you can show. The others can live in docs as headings, where a paragraph can make them specific. On the homepage they are costume.

Google's people-first content guidance is a clean test for the cut. The page should help someone do a task, from knowledge you have, without padding. The task is to judge the tool and try it. A slogan is padding that sounds like a point of view. A point of view you can keep is a constraint. "No telemetry without a switch you can see." That sentence should stay. The empowerment line should not.

## Cut claims the build does not honor

Remove "blazing fast" unless you are willing to show the condition and the measurement in a way you will update. Unqualified speed claims are slogans with numbers implied. This reader enjoys timing them. If you have a benchmark, put it in docs with the setup. If you do not, do not hint.

Remove logos you cannot connect to a technical constraint. A wall of brands without a decision is a sticker sheet. One true case, with the fork you refused, is stronger. If you have no permission to tell it yet, skip the wall. Absence reads as unfinished only to the team. To the reader it reads as a page that got to the tool faster.

Remove fake urgency. Limited beta spots, countdown bars, and "join thousands of developers" with a number you would not defend in an issue. State the license, the price shape, and the try path. Let them decide on the artifact. Urgency aimed at engineers tends to scan as a consumer trick, and it sticks to the product.

Remove the origin myth from the first view. A constraint you still obey can live, briefly, on the about page. A story about a hackathon weekend delays the screenshot. The screenshot is the reason the link was opened.

## Keep the screen and the try path

After the cuts, check that two things became clearer. A real screen, transcript, or snippet. A way to try the product, labeled with the mechanism. If a cut damaged either, restore it and cut something prettier. The ornament is the surplus. The artifact is the site.

Keep the limits in view. Where it runs. What the free try includes. What you do not parse. Limits are not clutter. They are how a skeptical reader trusts the remaining sentences. A short page can still say no. It should.

Keep one verb for the trial across the header, the first screen, and the pricing page. Install, sandbox, or try. A shorter site that uses three verbs is still confused. Pick the true mechanism and repeat it until the team is bored. Boredom means consistency. The reader experiences it as clarity.

Keep the docs one click away, with the word docs. Do not fold them into "learn" or "resources." This buyer has a place they expect technical truth to live. Meet them there. A short marketing site with excellent docs will outperform a long marketing site that restates the docs badly.

## Short does not mean a single scrolling pitch

Give the remaining pages distinct jobs. The homepage shows the mechanism and the try path. Pricing shows the unit, what is included, and what is not. A proof page shows one constraint and one decision. The about page names who maintains the tool. The contact page tells them what happens if they write, and points everyone else back to the trial.

A changelog should exist and read like a changelog. Versions, breaks, fixes. It is not a second blog of announcements about announcements. The blog can exist in the footer. It should not outrank the changelog in the header. Engineers who need to know if you are careful will read the notes. They will not read a thought piece first.

Each page should still make sense if the slogan is gone, because the slogan is gone. Read pricing alone. Read about alone. If a page depended on campaign language to feel finished, rewrite it until the facts are enough. Facts are the finish.

Nielsen Norman Group's observation that people often read only about a quarter of the words is a reason to stop writing, not a reason to add a summary of the summary. The quarter they read should be the mechanism, the limit, and the try path. Extra sections compete with those three. Delete the competitor.

## How to make the cut

List every block on the homepage. For each, finish the sentence "This helps an engineer…" If the ending is "feel inspired" or "understand our vibe," cut the block. If the ending is "see the failing migration" or "copy the install command," keep it.

Cover the page below the first screen. If the visible part shows the real tool and the try path, you have a spine. Reveal the next block only if it answers a doubt the first screen created. Telemetry. Runtime. A hard limit. Stop when a block exists because the layout felt empty. Empty is allowed. A false block is not.

Do the pass with someone who will use the tool and did not design the page. Give them permission to mark sacred lines. Sacred is a clue that the line is for the team. Ask what would be lost if it vanished. If the answer is the brand, check whether the mechanism already carries a voice. A precise tool has a voice. It does not need a second one hovering above it.

Ship the shorter page to a staging URL and send it to three engineers. Ask what the tool does and how to try it. Do not ask if they like the design. The first two answers are the review. If both come back clean, resist the urge to add the slogan back "for balance." Balance is how the mistake returns.

## Taste that still gets in the way

A site can be handsome and wrong. Careful type, a restrained palette, and a headline that could belong to any tool. The reader does not install the palette. They install the mechanism. Beauty that delays the snippet is the same class of bug as a layout that hides it.

Motion should not be required to understand the tool. A short transition can keep context. An intro sequence that plays before the command is a slower slogan. Honor reduced motion. The artifact and the try path should be present without animation. If the page only works as a film, the argument is trapped in the film. Write it in text and in a still.

Photography of conferences and loft offices, however well shot, still substitutes a scene for a screen. One true capture of the tool will do more. If you already paid for the loft, do not spend the hero on it. The hero is the output of the program.

Jokes and mascots can be part of a docs culture. On the first screen they often compete with the claim. Keep the joke if it is one line and the mechanism is still first. Cut the character that exists to seem friendly. Friendliness is a reply in an issue that reproduces the bug. It is not a costume on the homepage.

## A quarterly cut list

Repeat this pass often enough that new campaigns do not stick.

1. Remove slogans and tiles that do not name a mechanism.
2. Remove speed lines, logos, and timers you would not defend in public.
3. Confirm the first screen shows a real screen of the tool and a way to try it.
4. Confirm the header uses job words, with one stable trial verb.
5. Confirm pricing, docs, changelog, proof, about, and contact each do one job.
6. Open the first screen on a phone. If it survives, stop adding.

The shorter page will bother the team for a week. The bother is the missing slogan. The reader will not miss it. They will try the tool, or they will know why they did not.

A different buyer, with a different risk, needs the same honesty and a different first screen. Read [what the homepage has to prove for a fintech product](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-fintech-product) when the person on the other side is trusting you with money, not only with a build.

To see work edited down to the decision and the screen, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The public site should be able to stand that kind of cut.
